approachQuestion.prompt:
Cabinet balance. A read-only array rows contains r arrays of signed adjustment amounts. Return the sum of every amount in every row, including repeated amounts. Rows may be empty and may have different lengths. Row length and indexed access are provided directly. There are 1 <= r <= 100,000 rows and 0 <= N <= 200,000 amounts in total; each amount is between -1,000,000 and 1,000,000. All sums fit signed 64-bit words. Choose the fastest worst-case method, breaking equal-time ties by smaller auxiliary storage.

Example 1: Input: rows=[[4,-1],[],[7,2,-3]]. Output: 9.
Example 2: Input: rows=[[],[],[]]. Output: 0.

options.text: Visit every row and add each of its amounts into one running total.
options.feedback: Every stored amount contributes exactly once. Empty rows require no amount visits, and different row lengths are handled directly.

options.text: Copy all amounts in row order into one new flat array, then sum that array.
options.feedback: This handles every legal input, but the flat copy stores amounts that could have been added immediately. It has the same tight running time but more peak storage.

options.text: For each row, read exactly r amounts and add them.
options.feedback: The row count does not determine row length. For rows=[[4],[]], r is 2, so this attempts to read nonexistent entries.

options.text: Use the first row length as the number of amounts to read in every row.
options.feedback: For rows=[[],[5]], this reads no amounts and returns 0 instead of 5. Rows need not have equal lengths.

feedback.reason: Count the actual work across parts of unequal size; a nested layout alone does not imply a square number of visits.
details: Initialize a total to zero. For each row, iterate over exactly that row’s stored amounts and add each to the total. Return the total; allocate no flattened copy.

Three empty rows still require visiting three row headers despite containing zero amounts. Across nonempty rows, each amount belongs to exactly one inner traversal. Add row overhead to the number of stored amounts; multiplying row count by total amounts would count visits that never occur.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For visit-each-row-and-value, let r be the row count and N the total number of stored amounts. What are the worst-case time and auxiliary space? Row headers and their lengths are input. Include visiting empty rows.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

options.text: O(r + N) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(r + N) time, O(N + 1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Count r row visits plus N amount visits, with one running sum.
details: The outer traversal visits r row headers, while all inner traversals together visit N amounts. Thus work adds to O(r + N), even when N is zero. Only loop indices and one total remain live; there is no recursive stack or copied array.
“O(N + 1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This omits the r row visits: arbitrarily many empty rows still require traversal.
“O(r²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Inner lengths sum to N and are unrelated to r; one row may contain many amounts.
“O(r + N) time, O(N + 1) auxiliary space”: That storage describes flattening, which the analyzed method does not perform.
